query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ substrate preheating (350–450°C) combined with adaptive laser power modulation during laser powder bed fusion of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will reduce residual thermal stresses and enhance the mechanical properties of additively manufactured miniature components relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock with its as-supplied morphology, composition, and particle size distribution.
generation.intervention: Maintain the build platform at a controlled temperature of 350–450°C during printing, while simultaneously using adaptive laser power modulation to optimize energy input for miniature geometries.
generation.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion performed in a controlled atmosphere for miniature components, with a processing window set to a build platform temperature of 350–450°C, adjusted laser energy density, and post-build assessments at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients between layers leading to minimized rapid cooling and microstructural inhomogeneities, thereby lowering residual stresses and reducing defect formation (e.g., microcracks).
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build platform decreases the temperature differential between the melt pool and the substrate, thereby reducing thermal shock and stress; adaptive laser power ensures a more uniform energy distribution, facilitating a controlled solidification process and refined microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components will exhibit lower residual stresses as measured by X-ray diffraction, improved tensile strength and ductility from standardized mechanical testing, and overall a simplified processing regime compared to parts built under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.baseline: Components produced without substrate preheating and with constant, high laser power (i.e., standard high-thermal-load additive manufacturing setup).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to additively manufactured miniature components using laser powder bed fusion with the specified processing parameters; results may differ for larger-scale builds or other alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal combination of preheating temperature and adaptive laser power parameters for AlCrFeNiSi remains to be fully established, given potential variations in powder characteristics and thermal behavior during processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components using laser powder bed fusion: one set employing the intervention (build platform preheating at 350–450°C with adaptive laser power modulation) and a control set using conventional processing (room temperature platform with constant high laser power). Compare the residual stresses (via XRD), microstructure (using electron microscopy), and mechanical properties (tensile tests) between the two sets.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility via standardized mechanical testing
Microstructural features (grain size, presence of cracks, defect density) through electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention group does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >10%) in residual stresses and a measurable improvement in mechanical properties (tensile strength and ductility) compared to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The microstructural evolution and the mechanical properties have been characterized, and the following conclusions are drawn: Manufacturing of samples with a high density of 99.8% was achieved at a VED of 187.7 J/mm3. However, microcracks were also observed. Reducing the volume energy density using lower laser power reduces the occurrence of hot cracks but does not inhibit them in this study. Additive manufacturing currently facilitates new avenues for materials discovery that have not been fully explored. In this study we reveal how additive manufacturing can be leveraged to produce dispersion strengthened (DS), multi-principal element alloys (MPEA) without the use of traditional mechanical alloying or chemical reactions. This new processing technique employed resonant acoustic mixing to coat an equiatomic NiCoCr powder with nano-scale yttrium oxides. Then, through laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), the coated powder was successfully consolidated into 99.9% dense parts. Microstructural analysis confirmed the successful incorporation and dispersion of nano-scale oxides throughout the build volume. Furthermore, high temperature mechanical testing of the DS alloys showed significant improvements in strength and ductility over the baseline NiCoCr. As a result, this recently discovered processing route opens a new alloy design and production path that is synergistic between additive manufacturing and dispersion strengthening, possibly enabling a new generation of high-performance alloys.
